name: Promptforce
description: Loupe takes low resolution frames and scales it to higher resolution image using a tiny trained model, it also provides per tile quality score so the small portion of image that's hard to scale can be scaled using higher parameter model giving latency/cost advantages. It is a 241 KB model (59k parameters) that runs on your own machine: no AI service, no per-photo fee, and no photo leaves the computer. A hosted service would cost 1$ per 1200 photos resized.

name: Co-create
description: Cocreate: chat with an agent that edits a whole real-estate shoot, touches only what you asked for, proves it with a changed-pixel view, and recolours any wall in one click.

name: Verbalore
description: A daily video plan for people who know they should be on camera and never find the time. Verbalore researches what your market is posting about, writes the script in your voice, prompts you while you record, and edits the video for you with a graphic on every scene. A second half of the product watches the accounts in your CRM and turns each buying signal into a personal video note. Ideas. Seven use-case tabs (real estate, software developers, product marketers, GTM executives, C-suite, founders, general). Each pulls what people are posting in that niche from Reddit, Hacker News, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, LinkedIn and Facebook, scores every post against others on its own platform, drops off-topic ones, and writes five ideas. Each idea shows its evidence, one reference post picked by Jev with its hook / body / ending broken down, and a script in your voice. Daily email. A cron job queues the research each morning and a second one emails the five best ideas. Each has a button that opens the teleprompter. Studio. Camera preview, scrolling teleprompter (speed, size, mirror, pause on space), retake as often as you like, direct upload to storage. You can also upload an existing video. Record on your phone: the Studio shows a QR code. Scan it and the phone opens a full-screen recorder with the same teleprompter, no sign-in needed. When you press send, the take uploads straight to storage and appears in the desktop Studio on its own, ready to edit. The link is single-purpose, expires after two hours, and can only upload into its own folder. Edit. A worker normalises the take, gets word timings, cuts the transcript into scenes, and gives every scene a graphic: hook title, stat, list, quote, tip, code window, before/after, fact tiles, call to action. The scene plan is validated, so a scene can never ship without its graphic. Each use case offers its own edit themes (editorial, kinetic type, product UI, listing, terminal, boardroom). Library and posting. Preview, re-edit in another style, and post to up to 15 platforms through Upload-Post, now or scheduled. Signals. Watch any organization: add one, or paste a list of names and websites. For each one the engine reads the primary sources directly (SEC filings, the company's job board, its own website, GitHub) and also searches the news. Results are classified, de-duplicated, and ranked by fit and urgency, and each shows where it was found. You can also add a plain-language signal to watch ("opened a new office"). Pick a signal and a contact and it writes a 30 second note, you record it, and it goes out as a share page /v/<token> with view tracking. Brain. Notes, posts and pages you add. Scripts are written only from this, and a voice profile (tone, sentence length, repeated phrases) is learned from your own writing. A document can apply to everything or to one use-case tab, so real-estate notes never leak into developer content.

name: ShootAgent
description: ShootAgent takes a home listing all the way from a camera's raw shots to polished marketing videos that realtors can trust and post on social media. We have created a custom agentic pipeline that gives truly creative capabilities to a crew of specialized reviewer agents that truly vets a video how a professional would, and catches mistakes made by AutoHDR. ShootAgent compares each scene with the original shots and fixes the mistakes. Realtors can interact with an AI via chat to make edits that would otherwise take postprocessing professionals hours to make, like "remove the car," and we have created a verification loop that ensures accuracy from intent, and undoes any edit that fails its loop. It also checks everything in compliance! It then turns the approved photos into a narrated reel, with multilingual capabilities, so one listing reaches different audiences. For more creative reels, ten AI agents pitch, review and pick ideas, and 16 AI viewers and judges score the finished reels without knowing who made them.

name: BuildWright
description: BuildWright Know what you can build on an Austin lot before you buy it. Inspiration First-time builders, such as a family adding a backyard home (ADU) or someone planning a small fourplex, usually find out what their lot allows after they've already paid for it. Zoning, floodplains, permit history and the city's filing rules are all public in Austin, but they're spread across a dozen city maps and process pages written for professionals. In one industry survey, 75% of project owners went over budget and 77% finished late. We wanted to give the beginner the same picture a developer's team would put together, in minutes, with a source for every fact. What it does 1. Start on the street. A 3D street scene shows a finished house next to one under construction. One scroll flies the camera overhead and hands off to a map of Austin. 2. Find a lot, two ways. - "I have an address": type any Austin address, typos included. BuildWright matches it to its county parcel. - "Describe it": type something like "4 homes, avoid the floodplain". BuildWright ranks candidate spots across Austin and shows them as numbered pins on the map. 3. Five AI agents research the lot, shown as a crew of characters: - Zoney: zoning and codes. - Levee: flood and hazards. - Stamp: permit history nearby. - Foreman: the filing path for your project. - Fern: creeks and trees. Each one ticks through the real city layers it read, for example "FEMA flood zone: Hit (AE)" or "Building permits within 220 m: 4 found", then writes a plain-language summary that links to its sources. 4. Get the answer and the next steps. - A verdict up front, such as "A backyard ADU looks possible here, with a few checks first." - A step-by-step checklist that says why each step matters and links to the city source. - Local builders with photos, ratings and real reviews. - Pre-filled City of Austin permit forms to download. - An email and a phone call, drafted and sent only after you approve them. - Push back: say "only 3 homes" or "avoid the floodplain" and the research is redone. How we built it - Frontend: - Next.js 15, React 19 and TypeScript. - three.js, through React Three Fiber, for the 3D street. It's all built in code, with no model files. - MapLibre GL for the map. - A bold "neobrutalist" design system for the map and results pages. - Live city data: about 10 City of Austin ArcGIS layers queried in parallel for every lot: zoning, FEMA and city floodplains, building permits, wildfire areas, pipelines, the airport overlay, creek buffers and historic districts. - Address to parcel: the US Census geocoder, with Esri's World Geocoder as a fallback for misses and typos. The result is snapped to the Travis Central Appraisal District parcel, because geocoder points land on the street centerline and miss the zoning map. - AI agents: five Claude Haiku 5.5 calls run in parallel. Each sees only its own slice of the live facts and must answer in a fixed JSON format. Source links come from our code, not the model, so it can't invent a citation. If a call fails or takes longer than 12 seconds, that agent falls back to rule-written text built from the same facts. - Builders: Apify's Google Maps scraper finds 5 nearby builders, with photos, ratings and a real review. Results are cached, with a bundled fallback so the page never waits. - Documents and outreach: pdf-lib fills the permit forms. Resend or SMTP sends email and Twilio places calls. Both go only to approved recipients after an on-screen confirmation. - Art: the crew characters were generated with AI (in Figma) and animated with CSS. Tracks - AutoHDR: we built an image pipeline (lib/render.ts) that stitches the city aerial for the lot and corrects its tone and color. A version that places a 3D house on the lot is in progress, and its section on the results page is hidden until it's ready. - Antler: the buyer is the first-time builder, and the same flow screens lots for small developers. Austin is first; every city publishes the same kinds of map layers, so the agent pattern carries over. Possible revenue: a full permit-packet product, and referral fees from builders and surveyors. What's real and what isn't - Live: the city map data, the address-to-parcel match, the five AI agents, the builder lookup, and email and calls once keys are set. - The agent animation replays the exact layers each agent read after the research finishes. It isn't streamed live. - "Describe it" ranks a fixed set of Austin neighborhood points, not every parcel. - Permit forms are drafts, and nothing is submitted to the city. - There's no cost estimate or sale price yet. - Three demo addresses have saved city readings, used only if the city's servers are slow or down. - It's map research, not a zoning determination. Every finding links to its source so you can check it. Challenges we ran into - Geocoder points sit on the street centerline, outside every zoning polygon. That made real Austin addresses look like they were outside the city until we snapped them to the right parcel. - City servers can be slow, so we built fallbacks at every layer: per-agent template text, cached builders and saved demo readings. The demo never breaks. - Merging two teammates' apps (a 3D landing and a research pipeline) into one product on a hackathon clock. What's next - Real lot measurements: setbacks and how much can be built. - Cost estimates. - A check in code that every quoted fact appears in its source. - Hosting with a shared database. - Submitting to the city's permit system. - More cities. Built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, three.js, React Three Fiber, MapLibre GL, Claude Haiku 5.5 (Anthropic API), Apify, City of Austin ArcGIS, US Census Geocoder, Esri, Travis Central Appraisal District, pdf-lib, sharp, Resend, Twilio. Team Arpit Khavate and Fawaz Jamshed. Code: https://github.com/ArpitKhavate/Construction (branch combined-dev-v1)

name: Payment Intelligence
description: Problem Finance teams lose money and hours to payment friction nobody owns. Disputed card charges need evidence dug out of inboxes and written up by hand. Cross-border payments get declined by SCA checks or eaten by FX and cross-border fees because they went through the wrong card. Usage-based bills like AWS or Meta Ads keep growing until they auto-debit, sometimes pushing an account below its cash buffer before anyone notices. Who it helps Controllers, treasury managers and AP teams at fast-growing companies that run several corporate cards, multiple bank accounts and many usage-based vendors. Solution Payment Intelligence is one dashboard with three AI modules. The Auto-Dispute Concierge matches invoices, receipts and photos to disputed transactions using EmbeddingGemma 2 vector search and Gemma 3 vision. It then writes a chargeback letter and assembles the evidence package PDF. The Card Optimizer uses a probabilistic decision model to pick the card that clears SCA declines and avoids FX markup for each cross-border payment. Liquidity Guard classifies each bill line as fixed or usage-based and run-rates the variable ones to flag spikes. It also forecasts a 30-day P10/P50/P90 cash corridor per account with Mistral’s Timestral and recommends a pre-emptive sweep before a breach. Every model answer is checked against a deterministic engine, so the AI never sets the money figures on its own. Impact Dispute packages that took hours are ready in minutes. Declined payments are recovered and avoidable fees are cut. Cash shortfalls show up days ahead with a sized fix, instead of after the bank alert.

name: L1brary Labs - Cadence on Rho
description: Cadence on Rho — Work today. Own your payday. Cadence on Rho is an earned-pay prototype that brings employer payroll oversight, worker earnings, and controlled payout requests into one workspace. Workers see earnings accrue every 15 seconds during recorded shifts and can request access to earned pay up to three times daily within a weekly or biweekly cycle. Employers review requests, track available earnings and reserved amounts, and follow each payout’s status. Uncertain outcomes keep funds reserved, helping prevent duplicate payouts. The hackathon build adds this workflow to Cadence’s existing RLUSD payment engine, which supports wallet approval, durable payment records, and transaction reconciliation on XRP Ledger. The submitted demo uses simulated settlements. Rho staging access and test funding have been verified separately; connecting business funding checks, approved USD payouts, and bank reconciliation is the next integration step. The current prototype models one worker using browser-local records, with an illustrative payroll hold rather than calculated taxes. Cadence’s goal is to give workers greater flexibility over earned pay while keeping employers in control of funding, approvals, and payment accountability.

name: zeta-one
description: Zeta One: trust and risk intelligence for AI agents that move money Problem. Businesses are starting to let AI agents pay their bills. A known agent with valid permissions can still be manipulated: an invoice can carry hidden instructions, or a vendor’s bank details can be quietly swapped. Knowing who the agent is and what it may do doesn’t answer the question that matters: is this payment fraud anyway? Who it helps. Financial platforms like Rho, whose customers want agents to pay bills, and the finance teams and fraud reviewers who answer for those payments. Solution. Zeta One is a gateway that checks every agent payment before money moves. It asks who is acting, whether the business authorized the payment, and whether the payment looks like fraud. It then returns allow, challenge or block, with an evidence record saying why. When a customer disputes a payment, an assistant gathers the records and researches the vendor with cited sources, and a person decides. What makes it stand out. No model can talk money past a hard check. Code enforces identity, limits and hard risk flags. The right intelligence at each step. Rules decide routine payments. Jev, a typed decision model, and then a language model review only the uncertain ones. Customer friction counts as a cost, measured next to missed fraud. Data can stay in-house. We tested an open-weight model on a GPU we rented, as a fintech would run on its own server. Measured like an ML system, with frozen test sets, baselines and error analysis. Learning only from what people verify. A customer’s claim alone changes nothing. Impact. On 100 synthetic test cases, the rules alone let no fraud through but held 39 of 51 legitimate payments. Model review cut those holds to 14–19. The self-hosted model got 94 right for under $2 per 1,000 decisions. These are synthetic results, not production accuracy, and payments are simulated.

name: ReadyHex
description: ReadyHex enables Agents (and people) to query and organize geospatial data. You can set up custom workflows and an AI agent will help you do it. ReadyHex also supports has a data enrichment market where agents can be paid paid to enrich your geospatial data. The demo works best in the Austin TX area. Check it out here: https://readyhex.com/ Check out the demo here: https://www.loom.com/share/712e26dd4ce94fba8cfb65dd8ec7f42d

name: PayRun Guard
description: PayRun Guard is the safety check an AI agent must pass before it pays bills on Rho: it reads bills, vendors, balances and scheduled payments from Rho's sandbox API, applies 14 rules to each bill plus run-wide checks and a cash-floor plan (22 finding types), and cites the Rho record behind every hold. An agent loop plans, calls four tools (get run, pre-flight, request approval, pay), verifies each result, and can only pay a bill that passed pre-flight and carries a signed human approval token for that exact run, bill and amount; payments are idempotent and every decision lands in an append-only audit log. On this week's sandbox run, 3 of 13 bills ($896.50) are paid and 10 are held, while a naive agent without the gate would have made 9 improper payments worth $7,070.00. Payments are simulated (Rho's public API is read-only), the data is Rho's fictional sandbox company, and all code was written this week and is open source (MIT).

name: Stacks
description: stacks is a recipe book for coding agents. It gives your agent a proven tech stack setup for a new project, plus a checklist that must pass before the project counts as done. Today, an agent asked to start a project makes different choices each time and often skips the tests, linting, agent ops infra, and CI that a careful developer would add. stacks keeps the parts that don't change, like the layout and the rules, in the recipe, and the agent looks up current package versions itself, so the recipe never goes stale. For a developer, that means a new project with tests, battle tested tools and agent ops infra, provisioned and able to run in minutes instead of an afternoon of setup, and a passing checklist that shows the provisioned dev stack works before you start building on it.

name: Promptforce Maya
description: AI coding is haunted by three ghosts: Cost (the bill that keeps growing), Context (the agent that doesn't remember) and Control (the agent that goes rogue). Maya is an AI engineer that plans a build as features, has a team of models build each one in an isolated git worktree, and proves every change on a five-step check (build, vet, tests, full suite, held-out oracle) before it lands. Our Halloween show page draws the build at night, and every ghost on screen is a real event. In our showcase run Maya built an image upscaler for the AutoHDR track in 8 hours: 6 of 6 features proved, 38.29 dB on the test set against 34.69 for the standard method. The page also shows the 4 warnings the build went on past, in red, and all 50 times a person had to step in are logged.

name: Plans Guru
description: How many times have you tried to organize a group dinner with 4 or 5 friends, only to end up in a 40-message group chat debate where nobody can agree on a place, someone has a gluten allergy nobody remembered, and someone else only wants cheap eats under $15? Existing apps solve this by harvesting your personal preferences, tracking your location 24/7, and uploading your social graph to cloud servers. We believed there had to be a better way. We built PlansGuru — a privacy-first, 100% on-device AI dinner coordinator. It uses on-device LLMs and local multi-agent negotiation to find group consensus in seconds without a single byte of your preferences ever leaving your phone.

name: Pixie.so
description: With Pixie, a business demonstrates a process and gets a tested workflow its agents can run. Pixie is designed to self-heal when systems change and improve through feedback from verified runs, with built-in human-in-the-loop support. Pixie is the API for how a business works, enabling agents to get real business-specific work done across browsers, computers, APIs, and human-in-the-loop workflows.

name: Pinky Promise
description: Pinky Promise helps founders find out how they would actually work together before they pinky promise. Co-founder conflict is one of the most common reasons startups fail, and people still choose a partner after a few coffee chats. Pinky Promise looks at how you already work. A command on your laptop reads your git history and your Claude Code or Codex sessions. A ChatGPT or Claude export is read in the browser. If you have neither yet, a twelve-scene founder test gives the same kind of profile. You get a name for how you work, four letters, and the co-founder who would cover you. Invite someone and you both see one pair report: where you fit, where you will clash, and one small thing to try first. A program room suggests who in a cohort should try working together. Pairs are suggestions, never assignments. Your code and your chats stay on your device. You see the summary first, and nothing is saved until you approve it.

name: Ocypod
description: Ocypod is your petrochemical supply chain, in your pocket. It's an open-source Monte Carlo simulation of the global ethylene, polyethylene and MEG network: 549 real plants (crackers, coal-to-olefins, PE and MEG), 189 ports and 1,216 shipping, pipeline and rail lanes, all built from public data. The engine is written in kdb+/q and simulates the network day by day across 20 random draws in about 5 seconds per run. You describe a disruption, like a Gulf hurricane, a closed strait or specific plants going offline, and Ocypod shows where the shock travels, which regions and products get hit, how hard and for how long. Bruno, our AI agent, does real analyst work on top of the engine. He finds plants, defines custom scenarios, runs them against a baseline, writes q in a live worksheet, charts the results, stresses a sample trading book and produces an exposure brief you can save as a PDF. A guided demo builds all of that from scratch in under a minute. Ocypod is a scenario engine, not a price forecaster. What we're building is the network and the workflows around it, kept modular so the data and site parameters can be swapped for a company's own

name: OAI Enterprises
description: Scout Offline Proof tests local answers, extraction, and tool decisions under OS-enforced network denial and exports inspectable evidence. It is the first step toward measuring complete workflow outcomes against a shared standard online and offline, then improving configurations based on verified results. This means you get the same results on your daily workflows regardless of whether closed models/harnesses are available as offline tooling can be substituted without degrading output quality.

name: Kestrel
description: As many others are currently feeling, compute is the next bottleneck is agent workflows. Running parallel and always on agents quickly consumes system resources for most people. Current cloud agents do not have a solution to working with visual media. Game development in particular has not been possible thus far on cloud agents, so most people develop locally, this means only a few agents working on the game at a time. Kestrel solves this by giving agents their own desktop. Kestrel allows users to bring the harness they are used to, with ChatGPT and Claude logins, so you aren't stuck with us as token provider. Kestrel has remote streaming straight into the interface, so you can verify the work of your agents from your laptop, or phone, even if its running in a resource heavy game engine. With Kestrel, it is possible to scale agents that feel local, while working from anywhere.

name: Gangnam Style
description: townhall.town: Become a more informed voter with agents.

name: DevLens
description: DevLens is an evidence agent for a consented coding task. It turns one Claude Code session into a replay. A reviewer clicks a claim and sees the recording, the event, the code change, and the test result together. How it works: 1. Claude Code hooks append redacted events to a JSONL file. 2. A deterministic linker adds rule edges (prompted, edited, ran_test, failed, supersedes, verifies). Each edge names its rule and its evidence. 3. A separate sandbox re-run of the test is stored as its own event. It is never merged into the session's own test line. 4. A window recording of the terminal is synced to events by media offset. 5. The Replay page plays the recording. Clicking "first failed test" or "passing test" seeks the video to that event. 6. Three review questions come from fixed rules with event ids. No model writes them. The page also lists unknowns and what was not captured. The demo uses a real recorded session: the author ran Claude Code on a broken-API task, with consent, and screen recording had audio and camera off. There is also an experimental read-only adapter for T3 Code sessions, plus a recruiter view with a train-line journey of the session. Limits by design: no score, no rank, no hire verdict. Nothing here predicts job performance. DevLens shows evidence so a human can judge. Built with Next.js, TypeScript, Supabase, Vercel, and Claude Code.

name: Athlete Stories x OpenHealth
description: As an Athlete, we deserve the ability to relive, review, and share our journeys and progress for all of the effort we put in. The problem today is that even in the age of Agentic AI - our data and the stories and context behind them remain siloed. We have come together to create and explore two platforms that we plan to prototype at the AITX Tech Week Demo Day: 1. Athlete Stories (athletestories.org) - Which agentically integrates Data and then interviews Athletes and their supporters -- in order to produce and a Spotify-wrapped style recap of their story and journey 2. Open Health - Which agentically combines and presents data across an athlete's health and fitness apps and presents it in one comprehensive dashboard - so that every ounce of effort is visible and can be reviewed in the context of where and when it took place -- whether on top of a mountain, in the gym, or on the field

name: ALANI
description: Swarmageddon — a consent-first AI vulnerability-scanning swarm Problem. Every web app ships with holes — missing security headers, exposed .git and backup files, injectable inputs — and small teams rarely have the time or a specialist to find them before attackers do. Commercial scanners are slow, noisy with false positives, and opaque about what they actually touched. Who it helps. Indie developers, startup engineers, and security-curious builders who own a site and want a fast, trustworthy read on where it's weak — without hiring a pentester or risking damage to their own app. Solution. Swarmageddon is a consent-first, allowlist-gated swarm of AI agents. Point it at one URL you own; a coordinator locks scope, then specialist agents map the site and probe it in parallel — headers and cookies, exposed paths, and injection — streaming every step to a live dashboard. It is non-destructive by design: it sends tiny confirmation probes to prove a weakness exists, never destructive payloads, and re-verifies every finding against a fresh request before ranking it by severity. A server-side allowlist, a one-button STOP that halts the whole swarm mid-scan, request pacing, and an append-only audit log keep it safe and accountable. Impact. In seconds a developer gets a ranked, de-duplicated report they can act on tomorrow — each finding backed by real evidence and a full audit trail of exactly what was touched. It's a complex multi-agent pipeline, not a single-prompt wrapper: real recon, parallel execution, independent verification, and hard safety rails.

name: AI Car Technician
description: Torque turns a $20 OBD-II adapter and a browser tab into an AI car technician. In about 20 seconds it reads your car’s codes and live sensor data, runs its own tests, and explains the problem in plain English for your exact make. You get a step-by-step fix, plus real part numbers, prices and buy links found by live web search.
